274.title: Catherine of Siena
274.hook: a dyer's daughter who told popes what to do and nursed the plague-sick
274.carry: be who god meant you to be
274.howItsDone: Catholics honor Catherine as a saint and Doctor of the Church, with a feast day on April 29, and Christians of other churches read her letters and her book, The Dialogue, as models of prayer that turns into bold action.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was behovely, and Julian's great promise to end the week: all shall be well. Your line was a love bigger than the hurt.

A letter opens warmly, calling its reader father. A few lines later it tells him, plainly, that he is failing and needs to be braver. The reader is the pope. The writer is a young woman from Siena, in Italy, with no title, no money and no official role. Nobody appointed her to advise the pope. She did it anyway. And between letters, she was nursing the plague-sick and burying the dead. Today: Catherine Benincasa.
screen: `A WARM OPENING.` → `BE BRAVER.` → `WRITTEN TO THE POPE.`

segments.voice: Catherine was the daughter of a wool dyer in Siena, one of the youngest of a very large family; tradition says more than twenty children. As a girl she decided to give her whole life to God. Her family pushed back hard, wanting her married. She refused. She didn't join a convent; she joined a group of lay women connected to the Dominican order, and lived at home, in a little room, praying. Then, in her twenties, she went out. She cared for the sick and the poor of Siena, and when plague came back, she nursed the dying and buried the dead. People gathered around her, friars, nobles, ordinary people, calling her mamma. And she spoke up. The popes then lived not in Rome but in Avignon, in France. Catherine was convinced the pope belonged in Rome. She told him so in letter after letter, and even traveled to Avignon to say it in person. The pope did return to Rome; historians still debate how much she influenced that. Tradition says she learned to write only late; she dictated most of her letters to friends. A famous saying of hers is on posters and mugs: be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire. Those exact words aren't hers. They're a loose modern version of a letter telling a friend that if he were what he ought to be, he'd set all Italy on fire. But the idea is truly hers. She died at thirty-three. In 1970 the Catholic Church named her a Doctor of the Church. Her boldness came from prayer, and it went out as love.
screen: `A DYER'S DAUGHTER.` · `THE PLAGUE-SICK OF SIENA.` · `LETTERS TO THE POPE.` · `SET ALL ITALY ON FIRE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've kept quiet about that might need saying, to a friend, a boss, a family member, a group: not a rant, one honest sentence said with love. Picture saying it the way Catherine began her letters, warmly, and then clearly, and notice any fear, and any care underneath it. If you pray, you can ask for courage and kindness together.
Catherine Benincasa. The dyer's daughter from Siena who nursed the dying and told popes the truth, with love.
Your line: be who God meant you to be. Warm first, then clear. Day two hundred seventy-four, in the books.

275.title: The Imitation of Christ
275.hook: Thomas à Kempis's little book, read by Catholics and Protestants for five centuries
275.howItsDone: Many Christians, Catholic and Protestant above all, read The Imitation of Christ a few lines a day, often as part of morning or evening prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Catherine Benincasa, who nursed the dying and wrote to popes. Your line was be who God meant you to be.
screen: `BE WHO GOD MEANT YOU TO BE.`

segments.voice: Some books sit on a shelf and look important. Others get carried around until the spine cracks and the pages go soft. A small book written in the Netherlands in the early 1400s has been that second kind for nearly six hundred years. Soldiers carried it. Prisoners read it in their cells. Catholic saints knew it almost by heart. It has been translated into more languages than almost any book besides the Bible. And its author didn't even put his name on it. Today: ama nesciri.
screen: `A SPINE CRACKED FROM USE.` → `SOLDIERS, PRISONERS, SAINTS.` → `NO NAME ON IT.`

segments.voice: The author was almost certainly Thomas à Kempis, a quiet monk who lived most of his long life in a small community near Zwolle, in what's now the Netherlands. He spent years copying manuscripts, including the whole Bible by hand, more than once. He belonged to a movement called the Modern Devotion: ordinary believers and religious communities who wanted a simple, heartfelt, practical faith. Not arguments. Life. The book opens with a line of Jesus from John's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness." Then it asks, in effect: are you following? Not studying him. Following. It's full of short, sharp sentences. One says, roughly, that it's better to feel sorrow for your wrongs than to know how to define the word. Another says that on the day of judgment we won't be asked what we read, but how we lived. And one of its most famous lines is two words of Latin: ama nesciri. Love to be unknown. Do the good thing and let no one notice. Fittingly, Thomas never signed it; the book traveled for years without an author's name, and people argued over who wrote it. And it crossed every line the churches drew. Catholics treasure it. John Wesley, one of the founders of Methodism, put out his own English version. Many Protestants read it too, and so do some Orthodox Christians, though Orthodox writers have been more divided about it. Five centuries of Christians who disagreed about a great deal have agreed on this little book: the point is to walk the way he walked, quietly, every day.
screen: `A QUIET MONK NEAR ZWOLLE.` · `HE THAT FOLLOWETH ME.` · `AMA NESCIRI: LOVE TO BE UNKNOWN.` · `READ ACROSS EVERY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: The Imitation is often read a sentence at a time, so take this one: love to be unknown. Think of something good you did recently that you wanted someone to notice, and just notice the wanting, without judging it. Then imagine doing something good that nobody will ever find out about, and how that feels.
Ama nesciri. Latin for love to be unknown: Thomas à Kempis's own two words for doing good and letting no one notice.
Your line: follow quietly. Thomas never needed his own name on the book. See you tomorrow.

276.title: The interior castle
276.hook: Teresa pictures the soul as a castle of many rooms, God at the center
276.howItsDone: Christians, especially Catholics and Carmelites, read Teresa's Interior Castle as a guide to growing in prayer, and use her picture of rooms moving inward to describe the life of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ama nesciri, love to be unknown, from The Imitation of Christ. Your line was follow quietly.

A front hall gets all the traffic. The door opens and shuts, messages pile up, people come and go, and the little emergencies never stop. It's possible to spend years in the front hall of a life and never sit in the inner rooms. In 1577, a Spanish nun, sick and overworked, was told to write a book on prayer. She didn't know how to begin. Then, she said, a picture came to her. The soul is a castle. And many souls, she wrote, stay out in the courtyard. Today: las moradas.
screen: `LIVING IN THE FRONT HALL.` → `A NUN WHO DIDN'T KNOW HOW TO BEGIN.` → `THE SOUL IS A CASTLE.`

segments.voice: Teresa of Ávila was a Carmelite nun in sixteenth-century Spain: funny, stubborn, practical and brave. She traveled rough roads by cart to found new convents, clashed with powerful people, and wrote books on prayer that are still read. In The Interior Castle, she pictures the soul as a castle made of a single diamond or very clear crystal, with many rooms, the way Jesus said there are many dwelling places in his Father's house. In the King James Bible: "In my Father's house are many mansions." Teresa's rooms are arranged in seven sets, like rings, one inside another. At the very center, in the innermost room, lives God, the King, shining through the whole crystal. Here's the surprise, in Teresa's telling. The castle is already there. God is already at the center. Nobody has to build anything; the task is to go in. And the door into the castle, she says, is prayer. The outer rooms are noisy. Things from outside creep in with you, like snakes and vipers from the courtyard. That's normal. You keep walking. Further in, prayer grows quieter and simpler, and more is given than done. In the innermost rooms, Teresa describes a union with God she compares to rain falling into a river: you can't tell the waters apart anymore. But she's firm about one thing. The test of how far in you've gone isn't feelings. It's love of your neighbor, and humility.
screen: `A CASTLE OF CLEAR CRYSTAL.` · `GOD IN THE INNERMOST ROOM.` · `THE DOOR IS PRAYER.` · `THE TEST IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Picture a castle of clear crystal, light coming from its center, and yourself in a noisy outer room: your to-do list, your phone, today's worries crawling around. Don't chase them out; notice a door ahead, walk through it one room further in, where it's a little quieter, and stay there. If you pray, you can simply turn toward the light at the center.
Las moradas. Teresa's own title for the book: the dwelling places, the many rooms of the soul where God lives at the center.
Your line: there's a room further in. The castle is already there. That's day two hundred seventy-six.

277.title: The dark night
277.hook: John of the Cross: sometimes God feels absent, and that's part of the road
277.howItsDone: Christians in long dry seasons of prayer read John of the Cross, and spiritual directors use his idea of the dark night to help people keep praying when God feels far away.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was las moradas: rooms of crystal, God at the center. Your line was there's a room further in.

Some people of prayer describe a season like this, often only in a whisper. Prayer used to feel warm. Church used to move them. God used to feel close. Then, sometimes for no clear reason, it goes quiet. The words feel empty. Sitting down to pray is like talking into a closed room. They wonder if they're doing something wrong, or if it was all in their heads. A Spanish friar, once locked in a tiny prison cell by men of his own religious order, came to write about that very experience. Today's word: dark night.
screen: `PRAYER USED TO FEEL WARM.` → `IT GOES QUIET.` → `A FRIAR IN A PRISON CELL.`

segments.voice: John of the Cross was a Carmelite friar and a close colleague of Teresa, who you met yesterday. He worked with her to reform their order. Not everyone wanted reforming. Early accounts say some of his own brothers seized him and locked him in a cell in Toledo so small and dark he had to stand on a stool to read by the light from a slit in the wall. He was beaten. And in that darkness he composed poetry. After months, the story goes, he escaped at night by a rope of strips torn from blankets. Around that time came a poem that begins: on a dark night. Later he wrote a book explaining it, The Dark Night. His idea: at the start, God often feels close and sweet, the way a mother carries a small child. But at some point, God sets the child down to walk. The warm feelings dry up. Prayer feels dark and empty. John says this is not God leaving. It's God working in secret, loving you past your feelings, so that you come to love God for God, not for how God makes you feel. Bernard's four loves come back here. John calls this darkness a guiding night, a night more kindly than the dawn. The Psalms said it long before: "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." John distinguished this spiritual dryness from other kinds of suffering, and spiritual directors today add: if the darkness includes deep sadness or hopelessness, talk to someone, a doctor, a counselor, a trusted friend. Both can be true. Dark is not absent.
screen: `A CELL IN TOLEDO.` · `ON A DARK NIGHT.` · `GOD SETS THE CHILD DOWN TO WALK.` · `DARK IS NOT ABSENT.`

segments.voice: Gently remember a time when God, or meaning, or hope, felt far away, and hold it at arm's length without reliving it; you got through it, or you're in it now. Say quietly: dark is not absent. If you pray, you can simply sit in the dark with God, without needing to feel anything.
Dark night. John of the Cross's name for the season when God feels absent, and is still quietly at work.
Your line: dark is not absent. A flat season may be part of the road. Day two hundred seventy-seven, done.

278.title: Brother Lawrence's kitchen
278.hook: a monastery cook found God as near among the pots as at the altar
278.howItsDone: Christians, Catholic and Protestant alike, read Brother Lawrence and try to turn to God briefly and often through the day, especially during chores and ordinary work.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was dark night, John of the Cross's season when God feels far. Your line was dark is not absent.

A busy kitchen at dinner time. Pots boiling over. Somebody shouting for more bread, somebody else for the salt. The floor is wet, the oven is too hot, and the cook has a limp and a bad back. Not exactly a holy place. In a monastery in Paris, the cook was a clumsy former soldier who, by his own account, had a natural dislike of kitchen work. Yet visitors came away talking about his peace. He said he felt God as near among the pots as in church.
screen: `POTS BOILING OVER.` → `A CLUMSY FORMER SOLDIER.` → `AS NEAR AS IN CHURCH.`

segments.voice: His name was Nicolas Herman. He grew up poor in France, and accounts of his life say he went for a soldier and was wounded. His faith first woke up, he said later, at eighteen, looking at a bare tree in winter. Soon it would have leaves again, and flowers, and fruit. And all at once he felt the goodness and care of God. Years later he joined the Carmelites in Paris as a lay brother, taking the name Brother Lawrence. They put him in the kitchen for many years; later, when his leg got worse, he repaired sandals. He never wrote a book. After he died, a friend gathered his few letters and notes of their conversations into a little collection, The Practice of the Presence of God. Its idea is simple: talk to God all day, in plain words, not only at set times of prayer but while working. When the mind wanders, just come back, without fuss. The time of work, he said, was no different to him from the time of prayer. In the noise and clatter of the kitchen, with several people calling for different things at once, he felt God as calmly as if he were kneeling at the altar. He said he turned his little omelet in the pan for the love of God. When he'd finished, if there was nothing else to do, he'd pick up a straw from the floor, for love of God. Benedict had asked his kitchen monk to treat the pots like altar vessels; Lawrence did it at the stove. Nothing heroic. Every small thing, done with God in the room.
screen: `A BARE TREE IN WINTER.` · `A LAY BROTHER IN THE KITCHEN.` · `TALK TO GOD ALL DAY.` · `THE OMELET, FOR LOVE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Wash dishes as prayer, at a real sink or in your mind: the warm water, the soap, one plate at a time. With each dish, hold Brother Lawrence's thought that he was never working alone. If you pray, say a word or two to God, plainly, as to someone standing beside you; if you don't, give one plate your full attention.
Brother Lawrence. The clumsy former soldier turned cook who felt God as near among the pots as at the altar.
Your line: God among the pots. Work and prayer don't have to be two different rooms. See you tomorrow.

279.title: The inner light
279.hook: George Fox and the Quakers: there is that of God in everyone, found in silent waiting
279.howItsDone: In unprogrammed meetings, Quakers gather for worship in silence, speaking only when they feel led; in programmed meetings, found in parts of Africa and the Americas, they worship with pastors, hymns and sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Brother Lawrence, and his omelet turned for the love of God. Your line was God among the pots.

A plain room, with wooden benches facing each other. No altar, no pulpit, no music. People come in and sit down. And then nothing happens. Nobody leads. Nobody speaks. Five minutes. Twenty. A cough, a creaking bench, a bird outside. Then, maybe, someone stands, says a few quiet sentences, and sits down again. More silence. In a silent Quaker meeting, that is what worship looks like. It began with a restless young man in England.

George Fox was born in 1624, in a time of civil war and religious turmoil in England. As a young man he was desperate for spiritual answers. He went from minister to minister, and none of them could help. Then, he wrote in his Journal, when all his hopes in people were gone, he heard a voice that said, in his own old English: "There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition." His heart, he says, leapt for joy. Fox came to believe that God speaks directly to every person, not only through clergy or buildings. He pointed to the Gospel of John, which says of Christ: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." Every person. Friends came to call this the inner light, or the light within. Fox's followers called themselves Friends; others nicknamed them Quakers. They gathered in silence and waited for that light to speak. In a letter from prison in 1656, Fox urged them to "walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." Not only in the people who agree with you. In the jailer. The stranger. The enemy. Friends have traced some costly choices back to that conviction: work against slavery, prison reform, refusing to fight in wars. Today Quaker worship comes in different kinds. Some meetings still wait in silence. Others, in parts of Africa and the Americas, have pastors, hymns and sermons. Friends of both kinds speak of that of God in everyone.
screen: `SPEAK TO THY CONDITION.` · `THE TRUE LIGHT, WHICH LIGHTETH EVERY MAN.` · `SILENT WAITING.` · `THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.`

segments.voice: Sit in silence with one other person if someone is near, or picture someone you know sitting across from you: no talking, no phones. Don't try to make anything happen; just wait. If a thought feels like light, hold it, and if it's only noise, let it pass.
Quakers. The nickname for Fox's Friends, who wait in silence for God's light within every person to speak.
Your line: that of God in everyone. Even in the people who annoy you. That's day two hundred seventy-nine.

280.title: Seraphim of Sarov
280.hook: a Russian Orthodox hermit who greeted every visitor, my joy, Christ is risen
280.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians honor Seraphim as one of Russia's most beloved saints, and many greet each other with 'Christ is risen' through the Easter season, answering 'truly he is risen'.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Quakers: George Fox and the silent meeting. Your line was that of God in everyone.

Think about how you greet people. Hey. Hi. What's up. Usually it's automatic. Now imagine someone who greeted every single person who came to see him, rich or poor, sick or angry, a stranger or a sinner, the same way, every day of the year: bowing low, smiling, and saying, my joy, Christ is risen! Not just at Easter. In winter, in the middle of the week, to people he'd never met. That was an old monk in a forest in Russia, two hundred years ago.
screen: `HEY. HI. WHAT'S UP.` → `MY JOY, CHRIST IS RISEN!` → `EVERY DAY OF THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Seraphim was born in the 1750s in the Russian town of Kursk and became a monk at the monastery of Sarov. After years in the community, he went to live alone in a small hut in the forest, praying, reading the Gospels, working a little garden. Many stories are told about those years. People say he fed a wild bear from his hand. Tradition says that when robbers came, thinking he had money, he let them beat him nearly to death without resisting, and afterward asked that they not be punished. He recovered, bent over for the rest of his life. Then, after many years of silence, he opened his door. Crowds came, and every one heard the same greeting: my joy, Christ is risen! It's the Orthodox Easter greeting: one person says Christ is risen, the other answers, truly he is risen. Seraphim said it all year round, as if every day were Easter and every visitor his joy. He's remembered for a teaching often passed on in one line: acquire the spirit of peace, and thousands around you will be saved. The words vary in the telling, but the idea is clear. You can't argue or force people into peace. But a person truly at peace changes the room. People came to him anxious and left calm. In another famous conversation, he told a visitor that the true aim of the Christian life is to acquire the Holy Spirit. Not rules for their own sake: the Spirit, and peace with it. Look back at this week: Catherine's courage, the quiet Imitation, the castle, the dark night, the kitchen, the inner light, and now Seraphim. Each, in a different way, was learning peace.
screen: `A HUT IN THE FOREST.` · `HE DID NOT RESIST.` · `EVERY DAY IS EASTER.` · `ACQUIRE THE SPIRIT OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Think of the next person you'll greet, a family member, a coworker, the cashier, and picture them. Now picture greeting them as if they were a joy to you: not fake, just open, and notice what it does in you to see them that way. Let your breathing slow; that's where peace starts.
My joy. Seraphim's greeting to every single visitor, every day of the year, as if it were always Easter.
Your line: acquire peace. Peace in one person spreads. That's the week, day two hundred eighty.
